summary: Describes addressing and routing strategies for enterprises connected to multiple Internet service providers, intended to reduce the load such enterprises place on the global routing system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2260 describes ways for an enterprise connected to several ISPs to remain reachable without advertising every route everywhere. It compares route injection and non-direct EBGP, including their effects during failures.

questions: how to multihome with multiple isps
how does multihoming affect internet routing
how to multihome without growing the internet routing table
subtitle: Routing and address-allocation strategies for enterprises connected to several ISPs.

tldr.problem: Enterprises may connect to several ISPs for reliability, load distribution or better routing, but advertising a separate route for every enterprise can burden global routing.
tldr.mechanism: Each ISP lends the enterprise an address prefix. The enterprise normally advertises each prefix only to the ISP that allocated it, then uses route injection or non-direct EBGP to handle failures.
tldr.outcome: The strategies aim to reduce routing information in the default-free zone. They require careful address assignment, and changing providers may require renumbering.

facts.label: Provider-independent route overhead
facts.value: O(N), where N is the number of multi-homed enterprises

today: RFC 2260 is an Informational memo from January 1998. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Multiple Providers Affect Routing
sections.content:
An enterprise may connect to more than one Internet service provider to improve reliability, distribute load or obtain better routes across a wide area. The RFC assumes that requiring every router in the default-free zone to hold a route for every such enterprise would not scale.

The document focuses on addressing and routing strategies that reduce this overhead and require little coordination among ISPs. The strategies are described as applicable to both IPv4 and IPv6. Whether one ISP could meet the same needs is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple provider connections can help an enterprise stay connected when one path fails. The routing system still needs a way to carry those connections without requiring every router to track every enterprise separately.

sections.title: A Prefix from Each Provider
sections.content:
An enterprise connected to several ISPs receives a different address prefix from each one under the address-lending policy. It uses those prefixes to assign addresses within its network.

One possible plan assigns a host a prefix based on its topological proximity to an ISP connection. A host may use one prefix or addresses from multiple prefixes. The RFC notes that address assignment affects how traffic is distributed among provider connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider lends the enterprise an address range. The enterprise can assign addresses based on which provider connection is closest in its network.

sections.title: Advertising Routes When Links Work or Fail
sections.content:
When connectivity through all providers is working, each enterprise border router advertises to its directly connected ISP only the prefix that ISP allocated. The ISP can aggregate that route, keeping it out of the default-free zone.

If a router detects that connectivity through another ISP has failed, it can also advertise the prefix allocated by that ISP. The RFC calls this auto route injection. It describes using BGP information between enterprise border routers to detect the failure, or watching for the withdrawal of a selected route.
sections.plainLanguage: While all provider links work, each ISP hears only about the address range it lent. If another link fails, a border router can advertise the affected range through a working provider.

sections.title: Non-Direct Peering and Route Trade-Offs
sections.content:
To avoid adding routes to the default-free zone, the RFC describes non-direct EBGP peering between an enterprise border router and a router at an ISP connected to another enterprise border router. Direct routes are preferred. Traffic using a non-direct route is encapsulated and sent through the alternate enterprise connection.

This approach can produce a suboptimal route during failures. The RFC suggests combining it with route injection whose propagation is constrained using BGP communities. Other trade-offs include renumbering when an enterprise changes providers and the need to control how optional routes are distributed.
sections.plainLanguage: Non-direct peering can carry traffic through another enterprise connection without advertising extra routes globally. It may take a less direct path after a failure, so the memo also describes limiting route announcements.

sections.title: Alternatives and Security
sections.content:
The RFC compares its method with provider-independent address space and proxy aggregation. Provider-independent addresses cannot be aggregated with a provider's routes and can create routing overhead proportional to the number of multi-homed enterprises. Proxy aggregation requires additional coordination between ISPs.

Provider-assigned addresses mean an enterprise may need to renumber part of its network when changing ISPs. For non-direct EBGP sessions between routers more than one IP hop apart, the RFC says to use an appropriate BGP peer authentication mechanism. Other peering security is outside the memo's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The alternatives either add more routes or require more coordination between providers. This approach uses provider-assigned addresses, which can mean changing addresses when the enterprise changes providers.
